newsitem.title: USA: White House's Raines seeks US balanced budget deal.
newsitem.headline: White House's Raines seeks US balanced budget deal.

text.p: White House budget director Frank Raines said on Monday he would press the Republican-led Congress for a deal by February on an agreement to eliminate the deficit by 2002.
Raines said he would travel to Capitol Hill to meet with key Republican leaders this week, following up on President Clinton's budget meeting with them last week.
"I'm not making predictions that we'll succeed," he told a small group of reporters. "I'm simply saying that we'll put in a very serious effort to see if there is any possibility of agreement."
Clinton has expressed hope Republicans and Democrats can pick up where they left off early this year in budget talks, which broke off after 50 hours of Oval Office meetings.

Raines said he wants better relations with Republicans than in the past, but acknowledged important differences with them. For example, Raines opposes two proposals close to the hearts of Republicans: A broad cut in the capital gains tax and a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution.

For their part, Republicans have said they want to wait and see the president's budget proposal when it comes out the first week of February. The new Congress does not convene until early next year and the budget process takes 10 months.

"The assignment that I have is to see if there's a better path" to reach an agreement, Raines said. "It just strikes me that if you could find a less-adversarial way to approach the budget we might be more able to find useful solutions."

As a starting point, Raines said he would like to see if the two sides can agree on common economic assumptions instead of developing them separately. Differences in assumptions about the size of U.S. economic growth were a major sticking point last year.
Raines also endorsed the idea of commissions to work on long-term solutions to shortfalls in Medicare and Social Security.

Rains meets this week with the House and Senate budget committee chairmen, next week with House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, and after Thanksgiving in late November with Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican.
Raines said he will listen carefully to Republican arguments, but opposed a broad-based cut in the tax on capital gains.

"I personally don't think there's a need for a broader capital gains tax reduction," he said. "Usually capital gains reduction proposals are made because people believe it will increase prices on Wall Street and increase investments by corporations.

"We now have the highest prices on Wall Street in history and one of the highest levels of investment we've had in decades," said Raines, who worked as an investment banker for Lazard Freres and Co. in New York. "So it's hard to see what the problem is, to which the solution is to cut the capital gains tax."
The White House budget director was also upbeat about continued strong government receipts, which helped cut the deficit for the last fiscal year to $107 billion, the lowest since 1981.
Raines thought the deficit would drift up from that, but said the stronger receipts were not simply an anomaly.
"Some, if not all, of the extraordinary increase in receipts that were in last year's actual results will be repeated in 1997," he said.
